entities.summary:
The Battle of Mogadishu, also known as the Battle of Mogadishu (1993), was a pivotal event in modern African history that took place on October 3–4, 1993, in Mogadishu, Somalia. This conflict was sparked by a United Nations intervention in the Somali Civil War and involved a US-led coalition of forces. The battle resulted in a series of intense street battles between the Somali militias and the US-led coalition, ultimately leading to the withdrawal of UN forces. 

 The battle had significant consequences, including the withdrawal of UN forces from Somalia and the subsequent collapse of the UN's humanitarian efforts in the region. The conflict also marked a turning point in the US's foreign policy, as the US became increasingly involved in international interventions. 

 The Battle of Mogadishu was a defining moment in the history of modern warfare, as it showcased the limitations of the US military in urban warfare and highlighted the importance of coalition building in modern conflicts. The battle also had a lasting impact on the people of Somalia, who continue to suffer from the effects of the conflict. 

 The battle's legacy can be seen in the continued instability in Somalia, which remains one of the most fragile states in the world. The conflict also served as a catalyst for the US's more aggressive foreign policy in the 1990s and 2000s, as the US became increasingly involved in international interventions.
